rows.label: Share of money moved by a meta charity that donors wouldn't otherwise have given (new money)

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Effective Giving Incubation report
source.quote: the percentage of money raised that is counterfactual (i.e. would not have otherwise been donated) is about 50% of the total raised
source.note: Low: Ambitious Impact's own 35% for a charity evaluator (Better Futures Guide sheet, Main CEA!B34). High: our judgment for an organisation that mostly recruits new givers.

rows.explainer: Of the money a meta charity moves (an evaluator, a fundraiser, an effective-giving organisation), the share that would not have been given at all without it. The rest is shifted money: given anyway, now to a better charity. Every meta model on the site uses this one figure in our view (docs/normalization.md 2.8), in place of each evaluator's own: Ambitious Impact's 35% for evaluators, our earlier 40% for The Life You Can Save. 50%, from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Chance that a new, not-yet-proven meta organisation succeeds

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Establishing a livelihoods non-profit evaluator (2025): CEA, 'Probability of success'
source.note: Average of Ambitious Impact's three methods (comparable evaluators 63.5%, its incubated charities 50%, its statements on effective-giving organisations 53.75%); the range is the lowest and highest method.

rows.explainer: One chance of success for every meta organisation that has not yet shown results (an idea report's new charity). Ambitious Impact's own average of three methods, 55.7%; the range runs from its lowest method (50%) to its highest (63.5%). Established organisations with a track record (The Life You Can Save) take no such step.

source.note: Ambitious Impact values shifted money by the gain over GiveDirectly. Low: money shifted from ordinary charities that do little measurable good. High: from charities at GiveWell's funding bar, about 3× GiveDirectly's November 2024 estimate.

rows.explainer: Shifted money (given anyway, now to a better charity) is credited only with the gain: the value where it goes, less the value where it would have gone. rows.label: Share of the donations a meta charity's donors make that the charity caused (its own effect), when it has no donor survey of its own

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: Pledge counterfactuality coefficient 33% 26% ... Non-pledge counterfactual coefficient 28% 17%
source.note: Giving What We Can's donor surveys, the only published measurement of a meta charity's counterfactual influence on its donors' giving: best guesses 32.7% (pledgers) and 28.0% (other donors through its platform), conservative 26.0% and 17.0%; its raw 2023 pledger survey before the non-response discount, 40.2% (working sheet, 'Pledge counterfactuality coefficient'). Low: below the conservative non-pledge figure; high: above the raw survey.

rows.explainer: Of the donations a meta charity records or channels (through its platform, by its pledgers, by people it advised), the share that happened only because of it: the rest its donors would have given to the same effective charities anyway. A meta model reads its own donor survey where it has one (an observed input with its source), otherwise this figure. A different question from the new-money share: of the donations the charity caused, how much would not have been given at all (new) and how much was redirected from other charities (shifted). 30%, from 15% to 45%.

rows.label: Share of new giving pledgers recording donations in their first pledge year

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: y₀ 59.4% 0.0076 7.90e-13 Initial percentage of pledgers recording donations
source.note: Exponential decay to a floor fitted to 10% Pledge cohorts 2017–2023 by years since pledging; range about two standard errors.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 1 of 3: of people who take a lifetime giving pledge, the share giving (recorded) in their first year. With the decay and the floor: share giving in year t = floor + (first year − floor) × (1 − decay)^t. The only published cohort data on how pledges hold up; every pledge model reads it unless the organisation publishes its own.

rows.label: Yearly fall in the share of pledgers still giving, above the long-term floor

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: r 48.0% 0.0276 1.20e-07 Annual decay rate of the non-floor component
source.note: Range about two standard errors.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 2 of 3: each year the share of pledgers giving above the floor falls by about half.

rows.label: Long-term share of pledgers still giving (floor)

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: c 27.8% 0.0076 3.55e-10 Long-term floor percentage of pledgers recording donations
source.note: Fitted on up to 10 years of data. Low: our judgment that the share may fall further after year 10 (the report: 'it is entirely possible that the percentage of reporting pledgers will drop again'); high: about two standard errors and a half.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 3 of 3: the share of pledgers who keep giving for good, about 28%. The report finds the decline levels off at 25–30% for older cohorts.

rows.label: Giving What We Can 2023–2024: share of its donors' giving that went to charities and funds it rates high-impact

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: Pledge effectiveness coefficient 77% 50% ... Non-pledge effectiveness coefficient 99.7% 73%
source.note: Weighted by the money each stream moves in our model of it at the defaults (pledges $26.8M, other platform giving $7.0M, 2023–2024): (26.80 × 0.774 + 7.03 × 0.997) / 33.83 = 0.82; weighted by recorded donations instead it is 0.83. Low: the same with the conservative coefficients (only charities it recommended): (26.80 × 0.502 + 7.03 × 0.733) / 33.83 = 0.55. High: its top-100 pledge recipients' best-guess rate (0.911), rounded down.

rows.explainer: Of what Giving What We Can's donors gave, the share to recipients its own review classes as top or standout (its or an impact-focused evaluator's recommendations, effective-giving organisations); the rest went to charities it couldn't place, valued as an ordinary charity in its destination mix.
